title: Boolean Indexing and Filtering
goal: Filter arrays with masks, replace values with where and test membership with isin.

topics.title: Filter with a mask
topics.body: A comparison builds a boolean array; indexing with it keeps the True positions and returns a new array of the passing values.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([55, 72, 38])
print(a[a >= 60])

topics.title: np.where chooses without a loop
topics.body: where(condition, x, y) returns x where the condition is True and y where it is False, so a label column is one call.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 5, 3])
print(np.where(a > 2, 'big', 'small'))

topics.title: Membership with isin
topics.body: isin answers "is each element in this list?" and returns a mask, which composes with other masks for multi-condition filters.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])
print(np.isin(a, [2, 4]))

debug.title: A mask shorter than the array
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a[[True, False]])
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a[[True, False, True]])
debug.error: IndexError: boolean index did not match indexed array along axis 0

debug.title: where with only one branch
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(np.where(a > 1, 'yes'))
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(np.where(a > 1, 'yes', 'no'))
debug.error: ValueError: either both or neither of x and y should be given

title: Sorting, Searching and Set Operations
goal: Sort along an axis, recover order with argsort, locate insertion points and compare sets of values.

topics.title: sort and argsort
topics.body: np.sort returns a sorted copy while argsort returns the INDICES that would sort the array — the second is what you use to reorder parallel arrays.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([3, 1, 2])
print(np.sort(a), np.argsort(a))

topics.title: searchsorted
topics.body: searchsorted finds the insertion index that keeps a sorted array ordered, which is how you bucket a value without scanning.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 3, 5])
print(np.searchsorted(a, 4))

topics.title: Unique values and set operations
topics.body: unique returns sorted distinct values and intersect1d/union1d/setdiff1d answer the set questions directly on arrays.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 2, 3])
print(np.unique(a), np.intersect1d(a, [2, 4]))

debug.title: Sorting along an axis that does not exist
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[3, 1], [2, 4]])
print(np.sort(a, axis=2))
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[3, 1], [2, 4]])
print(np.sort(a, axis=1))
debug.error: AxisError: axis 2 is out of bounds for array of dimension 2

debug.title: a.sort() returns None
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([3, 1, 2])
print(a.sort())
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([3, 1, 2])
a.sort()
print(a)
debug.error: prints None — ndarray.sort() sorts in place and returns nothing

title: Copies, Views, Strides and Memory
goal: Tell a view from a copy, prove sharing with shares_memory, and read strides and contiguity.

topics.title: view shares, copy does not
topics.body: a.view() shares the same buffer so a write through the view changes the original; a.copy() allocates new memory and leaves the original alone.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
v = a.view()
c = a.copy()
v[0] = 9
print(a, c)

topics.title: Prove sharing with shares_memory
topics.body: Slicing usually returns a view, but an explicit copy never shares; shares_memory answers the question with a real check instead of a guess.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
print(np.shares_memory(a, a[1:3]), np.shares_memory(a, a.copy()))

topics.title: Strides describe memory steps
topics.body: strides are the bytes to move per axis; a (2, 3) int64 array steps 24 bytes per row and 8 bytes per column, which is why layout affects speed.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a.strides)

debug.title: Adding to a view rebound the name
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
b = a.view()
b = b + 1
print(a)
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
b = a.view()
b += 1
print(a)
debug.error: prints [0 1 2 3] — b + 1 created a new array, so the view was lost

debug.title: Strides are read-only
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
a.strides = (1,)
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
print(a.strides)
debug.error: AttributeError: attribute 'strides' of 'numpy.ndarray' objects is not writable

title: Random Number Generation
goal: Use default_rng, reproduce runs with a seed, and sample from the common distributions.

topics.title: default_rng and reproducibility
topics.body: default_rng(seed) returns a Generator; the same seed reproduces the same stream on every run, which is what makes a simulation debuggable.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
a = rng.integers(0, 10, 3)
print(len(a), a.min() >= 0, a.max() < 10)

topics.title: Normal draws
topics.body: rng.normal(loc, scale, size) samples a Gaussian; rounding the printed values keeps a demo readable without changing the data.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
print(rng.normal(0, 1, 2).shape)

topics.title: choice and shuffle
topics.body: choice samples with replacement by default (replace=False for a draw without repeats) and shuffle reorders an array in place.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
print(len(np.unique(rng.choice([1, 2, 3], 2, replace=False))))

title: Linear Algebra
goal: Multiply matrices, solve systems with solve instead of inv, and read determinant and eigenvalue output.

topics.title: Matrix multiplication
topics.body: The @ operator (and np.matmul) performs matrix multiplication, not elementwise multiplication; multiplying by an identity returns the same matrix.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
B = np.eye(2)
print(A @ B)

topics.title: Solve instead of invert
topics.body: np.linalg.solve(A, b) solves Ax = b directly and is numerically safer and faster than computing inv(A) @ b.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[2., 1.], [1., 3.]])
b = np.array([5., 10.])
print(np.linalg.solve(A, b))

topics.title: Determinant and eigenvalues
topics.body: det tells you whether a matrix is singular and eigvals returns the eigenvalues; for a diagonal matrix those eigenvalues are the diagonal entries.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[2., 0.], [0., 3.]])
print(np.linalg.det(A), np.linalg.eigvals(A).real)

debug.title: A singular system
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[1, 2], [2, 4]])
b = np.array([1, 2])
print(np.linalg.solve(A, b))
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[1, 2], [2, 5]])
b = np.array([1, 2])
print(np.linalg.solve(A, b))

debug.title: Elementwise product is not a matrix product
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(np.linalg.inv(A) * A)
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(np.linalg.inv(A) @ A)
debug.error: no error, but * multiplies elementwise; only @ gives the identity
